# Purpose

This study analyses supplied FuelWatch raw exports for January 2023–August 2026.Data for September 2026 is outside the scope of this study.
Each row represents a notified price at a specific site for a given product and date, rather than actual sales volume or transaction value. Prices are in cents per litre. 

Core Research Questions:
1. How do prices vary by date, product, brand and region?
2. Can non-price attributes identify relatively cheap regular unleaded petrol (ULP) records? Specifically, does training the model on historical August data outperform training on data from May to July 2026—that is, is it better to use year-over-year (YoY) or month-over-month (MoM) data for training?
3. Which price profiles distinguish ULP sites within a common observation window?

These are observational associations; the impact of wars, exchange rates, and crude oil fluctuations cannot be identified from this dataset alone. Where external factors cause changes, I will provide reliable sources. Additionally, no precomputed trend, weekly, or monthly price tables from FuelWatch were used in this study.


```{r setup}
required <- c("data.table","ggplot2","e1071","pROC","ROCR","lime","gridExtra","cluster","knitr")
missing <- required[!vapply(required, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly=TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) stop("Run setup.R. Missing: ", paste(missing, collapse=", "))
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
setDTthreads(2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=TRUE,
                     fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5, dpi=120)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size=12))
set.seed(params$seed)
start_date <- as.Date("2023-01-01")
test_start <- as.Date("2026-08-01")
end_date <- as.Date("2026-08-31")
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings=FALSE)
tab <- function(x, digits=3) knitr::kable(as.data.frame(x), digits=digits)
```

# Provenance and data quality

Source: FuelWatch historical retail price files published by the Western Australian
Government, downloaded from <https://www.fuelwatch.wa.gov.au/retail/historic> on
25 September 2026. One CSV per month was downloaded for January 2023 to September
2026 and stored unchanged in `datasets/`. The manifest records filenames, MD5
hashes, dates, counts and inspection date, to verify that the same
files were used.

```{r import}
# Read a monthly file. Require the schema; ignore only entirely empty extra columns.
read_month <- function(path) {
  fields <- c("PUBLISH_DATE","TRADING_NAME","BRAND_DESCRIPTION","PRODUCT_DESCRIPTION",
              "PRODUCT_PRICE","ADDRESS","LOCATION","POSTCODE","AREA_DESCRIPTION",
              "REGION_DESCRIPTION")
  x <- fread(path, colClasses="character", na.strings=c("","NA"))
  if (length(setdiff(fields,names(x)))) stop("Missing fields in ",path)
  extra <- setdiff(names(x), fields)
  if (length(extra) && any(vapply(x[,..extra],
      function(z) any(!is.na(z) & trimws(z)!=""), logical(1)))) {
    stop("Unexpected nonempty columns: ",path)
  }
  x <- x[,..fields]
  x[,source_file:=basename(path)]
  x
}
paths <- sort(list.files("datasets",
  pattern="^FuelWatchRetail-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4}\\.csv$", full.names=TRUE))
if (!length(paths)) stop("No input CSV files.")
file_month <- as.Date(sub("FuelWatchRetail-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{4})\\.csv",
                         "\\2-\\1-01",basename(paths)))
in_scope <- file_month >= start_date & file_month <= test_start
if (!setequal(file_month[in_scope],seq(start_date,test_start,by="month")) ||
    anyDuplicated(file_month[in_scope])) stop("Expected one file for each of 44 months.")
excluded_files <- basename(paths[!in_scope])
paths <- paths[in_scope]
raw <- rbindlist(lapply(paths,read_month),use.names=TRUE)
raw[,date:=as.Date(PUBLISH_DATE,"%d/%m/%Y")]
if (anyNA(raw$date)) stop("Unparseable dates; inspect source before proceeding.")
manifest <- raw[,.(rows=.N, first=min(date), last=max(date), days=uniqueN(date)),
                by=source_file]
manifest[,md5:=unname(tools::md5sum(file.path("datasets",source_file)))]
manifest[,inspected_on:=as.character(Sys.Date())]
manifest[,expected_start:=as.Date(sub("FuelWatchRetail-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{4})\\.csv",
                                     "\\2-\\1-01",source_file))]
manifest[,next_month:=as.Date(format(expected_start+32,"%Y-%m-01"))]
manifest[,complete:=first==expected_start & last==next_month-1 &
                      days==as.integer(next_month-expected_start)]
if (any(!manifest$complete)) stop("Incomplete month; inspect manifest.")
if (any(raw$date < start_date | raw$date > end_date)) stop("Dates outside scope.")
fwrite(manifest,"outputs/input_manifest.csv")
tab(manifest[,.(source_file,rows,first,last,days,complete)])
cat("Excluded by study scope:",paste(excluded_files,collapse=", "))
```

```{r inspect}
head(raw)
str(raw)
summary(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$PRODUCT_PRICE)))
```

Text import preserves postcodes. Dates/prices are explicitly converted. Early
exports have a trailing empty field; the reader verifies it is empty.
I used `data.table::fread()` instead of the base `read.csv()` from Lab 5. Both
read the same flat files, and `fread(colClasses="character")` does the same job
as `read.csv(colClasses="character")`, but it is much faster for 44 files and
3.8 million rows. All changes to the data and code are logged in `CHANGELOG.txt`.

**What the first look tells me.** Each row is one site, one product, one day.
`head()` shows that a single station (e.g. 53 Mile Roadhouse in Pinjarra) appears
several times on the same date, once per fuel it sells, so the "unit" for most
analysis has to be site × product × date, not the row on its own. `str()` shows
that everything comes in as text, which is what I wanted: postcodes like 6208
stay as labels instead of becoming numbers, and the date (`dd/mm/yyyy`) and price
need explicit conversion. The price `summary()` runs from 109.7 to 450.0 c/L with
a median of 191.9 and a mean of 195.9. The mean sitting above the median hints at
a right tail, and since this mixes LPG, ULP and diesel together, I did not read
too much into it until the products were separated below.

## Cleaning policy

Standardise whitespace and case; replace missing categories with UNKNOWN.
Do not merge similar brands without evidence. Identify sites by address, locality
and postcode; use trading name if address is absent. Where multiple records share
an address/product/date, append trading name to that address for every period.
This retains co-located named businesses without averaging their prices. A name
change at an ambiguous address or a location change can create a new key;
coverage changes are not automatically business openings or closures.

Remove unusable prices and exact canonical duplicates, with a 5% removal guard.
Conflicting site/product/date rows cause an explicit stop. Flag but retain
positive extreme prices: remote locations can legitimately be expensive.

```{r clean}
clean_text <- function(x) {
  y <- toupper(gsub("\\s+"," ",trimws(x)))
  y[is.na(y)|y==""] <- "UNKNOWN"
  y
}
normalisation <- rbindlist(lapply(c("BRAND_DESCRIPTION","LOCATION","REGION_DESCRIPTION"),
 function(nm) data.table(field=nm,raw_levels=uniqueN(raw[[nm]]),
                        clean_levels=uniqueN(clean_text(raw[[nm]])))))
missing_audit <- data.table(field=names(raw),
                           missing=vapply(raw,function(z) if (is.character(z)) sum(is.na(z)|z=="") else sum(is.na(z)),numeric(1)))
d <- raw[,.(date,site_name=clean_text(TRADING_NAME),brand=clean_text(BRAND_DESCRIPTION),
  product=clean_text(PRODUCT_DESCRIPTION),price=suppressWarnings(as.numeric(PRODUCT_PRICE)),
  address=clean_text(ADDRESS),location=clean_text(LOCATION),postcode=clean_text(POSTCODE),
  area=clean_text(AREA_DESCRIPTION),region=clean_text(REGION_DESCRIPTION),source_file)]
raw_n <- nrow(d)
bad <- !is.finite(d$price)|d$price<=0
invalid_n <- sum(bad)
d <- d[!bad]
canonical <- setdiff(names(d),"source_file")
before <- nrow(d)
d <- unique(d,by=canonical)
duplicate_n <- before-nrow(d)
d[,site:=paste(address,location,postcode,sep=" | ")]
d[address=="UNKNOWN",site:=paste(site_name,location,postcode,sep=" | ")]
address_collisions <- d[, .N, by=.(site,product,date)][N>1]
ambiguous_addresses <- unique(address_collisions$site)
site_identity_audit <- d[site %in% ambiguous_addresses,
  .(records=.N,names=paste(sort(unique(site_name)),collapse="; ")),by=site]
fwrite(site_identity_audit,"outputs/site_identity_audit.csv")
# Apply the same disambiguation throughout the study, not only on collision dates.
d[site %in% ambiguous_addresses,site:=paste(site,site_name,sep=" | ")]
conflicts <- d[, .N, by=.(site,product,date)][N>1]
if (nrow(conflicts)) {
  fwrite(conflicts,"outputs/conflicting_records.csv")
  stop("Conflicting site/product/date rows; review outputs/conflicting_records.csv.")
}
quality <- data.table(step=c("Raw rows","Invalid price removed","Duplicates removed","Clean rows"),
                      rows=c(raw_n,invalid_n,duplicate_n,nrow(d)))
drop_rate <- (invalid_n+duplicate_n)/raw_n
if (drop_rate>.05) stop("Cleaning removal exceeds 5%; review decisions.")
d[,":="(year=as.integer(format(date,"%Y")), month=as.integer(format(date,"%m")),
        month_date=as.Date(format(date,"%Y-%m-01")),day=as.integer(format(date,"%d")),
        weekday=factor(as.POSIXlt(date)$wday,levels=0:6,
                       labels=c("Sun","Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat")))]
bounds <- d[,.(q1=quantile(price,.25),q3=quantile(price,.75)),by=product]
d <- merge(d,bounds,by="product",all.x=TRUE,sort=FALSE)
d[,extreme:=price<q1-3*(q3-q1)|price>q3+3*(q3-q1)]
extremes <- d[,.(records=.N,flagged=sum(extreme),minimum=min(price),maximum=max(price)),by=product]
tab(quality); tab(normalisation); tab(missing_audit); tab(extremes)
cat(sprintf("Cleaning removal: %.4f%%",100*drop_rate))
fwrite(quality,"outputs/cleaning_audit.csv")
rm(raw)
invisible(gc())
```

```{r quality-plot}
ggplot(extremes,aes(product,flagged/records)) + geom_col(fill="#c36b39") +
 labs(title="Extreme-price flags are a review aid, not a deletion rule",
      x="Product",y="Fraction beyond product-wide 3-IQR fences")
```

The data turned out to be cleaner than I expected: no missing values in any
field, no unparseable prices, and no exact duplicates, so no rows were dropped
(well inside the 5% limit). Normalising case and spacing did not reduce the
number of brand, location or region levels either, which suggests FuelWatch
already standardises these fields. The real problem was site identity: some
addresses host more than one trading name on the same day, which is why the
disambiguation step above was needed before any site-level work.

LPG has the largest share of extreme-price flags (about 6% of records, from a
small base of 98 sites), followed by brand diesel and diesel (about 3.5% and
2.5%), while E85 has none. I kept these rows. The high values are mostly
from remote areas where 300+ c/L is plausible, and deleting them would make the
Kimberley and Pilbara look cheaper than they really are.

## Further checks before trusting the data

Zero removed rows does not mean zero problems, so I ran a few more checks on
things that would not show up as missing values or duplicates.

```{r cleaning-checks}
# 1. Brand names that might be spelling variants of one another (same first word).
brand_first <- unique(d[,.(brand)])[,first_word:=sub(" .*","",brand)]
brand_variants <- brand_first[,.(brands=.N,names=paste(sort(brand),collapse="; ")),by=first_word][brands>1]
tab(brand_variants)
# 2. Sites that change brand during the study (rebranding).
site_brand <- unique(d[,.(site,date,brand)])[order(site,date)]
site_brand[,switched:=brand!=shift(brand),by=site]
switches <- site_brand[switched==TRUE]
switch_month <- switches[,.(switches=.N),by=.(month_date=as.Date(format(date,"%Y-%m-01")))]
multi_brand_sites <- uniqueN(switches$site)
# 3. Which products exist in which year.
product_years <- dcast(d[,.N,by=.(product,year)],product~year,value.var="N",fill=0)
tab(product_years)
# 4. Price precision and postcode format.
format_checks <- data.table(
  check=c("Prices with at most one decimal place","Postcodes matching 6xxx"),
  share=c(mean(abs(d$price*10-round(d$price*10))<1e-6),mean(grepl("^6[0-9]{3}$",d$postcode))))
tab(format_checks)
# 5. Are extreme prices really concentrated in remote regions?
extreme_region <- d[,.(records=.N,flagged_share=mean(extreme)),by=region][order(-flagged_share)]
tab(extreme_region)
ggplot(switch_month,aes(month_date,switches))+geom_col(fill="#167c80")+
 labs(title="Brand changes at the same site, by month",
      subtitle=sprintf("%d sites carry more than one brand during the study",multi_brand_sites),
      x=NULL,y="Sites changing brand")
```

```{r cleaning-checks-text, results='asis'}
top_extreme <- extreme_region[1:3]
cat(sprintf("Brand names look consistent: %d first-word groups contain more than one brand, and these are separate brand labels rather than spelling variants (for example *%s*), so I did not merge any of them. ",
 nrow(brand_variants),if (nrow(brand_variants)) brand_variants$names[1] else "none"))
cat(sprintf("**%d sites change brand** at least once (%d brand changes in total). I keep the site key based on the address, so a rebranded station stays the same site, and the brand column always shows the brand on that day. This matters for the model, because a site's brand is not fixed over time.\n\n",
 multi_brand_sites,nrow(switches)))
cat(sprintf("%.1f%% of prices have at most one decimal place and %.1f%% of postcodes match the WA 6xxx format, so there are no unit or formatting errors hiding in the numbers. The product table shows that the set of fuels is not constant across years, which is one more reason to model a single product (ULP) only.\n\n",
 100*format_checks$share[1],100*format_checks$share[2]))
cat(sprintf("Extreme-price flags are most common in %s (%.1f%%), %s (%.1f%%) and %s (%.1f%%), compared with %.1f%% in Metro. This supports keeping them: they come from remote areas, not from data errors.\n",
 top_extreme$region[1],100*top_extreme$flagged_share[1],top_extreme$region[2],100*top_extreme$flagged_share[2],
 top_extreme$region[3],100*top_extreme$flagged_share[3],100*extreme_region[region=="METRO",flagged_share]))
```

# Exploratory analysis

Averages weight site-days equally, not litres sold. Product selection and
modelling samples below are analytical subsets, separate from quality removals.

```{r summaries}
monthly <- d[,.(mean_price=mean(price),median_price=median(price),records=.N,sites=uniqueN(site)),
              by=.(month_date,product,region)]
daily <- d[,.(mean_price=mean(price),records=.N),by=.(date,product,region)]
brand_month <- d[,.(mean_price=mean(price),records=.N),by=.(month_date,product,region,brand)]
all_month <- d[,.(mean_price=mean(price),records=.N,sites=uniqueN(site)),by=.(month_date,product)]
tab(d[,.(records=.N,sites=uniqueN(site),mean_price=mean(price),
          median_price=median(price),sd_price=sd(price)),by=product])
```

```{r trends}
ggplot(all_month,aes(month_date,mean_price,colour=product)) + geom_line(linewidth=.7) +
 labs(title="Monthly average notified prices",subtitle="Computed from raw exports; not sales-weighted",
      x=NULL,y="Price (cents/litre)",colour="Product")
```

Most products move together, which fits the idea that a shared wholesale cost
drives them. The gap between them is fairly stable: LPG is clearly the cheapest
(about 140 c/L on average), ULP sits around 185, and diesel, PULP and 98 RON
cluster around 198–206. E85 is the odd one out: it is the most expensive and
almost flat, but it only has 16 sites, so I would not draw conclusions from it.
The most striking feature is the jump in March 2026, where ULP goes from about
170 to 224 c/L in one month and diesel goes even higher in April. I come back to
this in the price-shock section, because it matters for the training-data question.

```{r coverage}
coverage <- d[product=="ULP",.(sites=uniqueN(site),records=.N),by=month_date]
ggplot(coverage,aes(month_date,sites)) + geom_line(colour="#167c80") + geom_point(size=1.3) +
 labs(title="ULP site coverage over time",x=NULL,y="Observed sites")
early_sites <- d[product=="ULP"&month_date==as.Date("2026-04-01"),unique(site)]
late_sites <- d[product=="ULP"&month_date==as.Date("2026-05-01"),unique(site)]
common_sites <- intersect(early_sites,late_sites)
coverage_changes <- data.table(measure=c("April sites","May sites","Shared",
                               "May only","April only"),
 n=c(length(early_sites),length(late_sites),length(common_sites),
     length(setdiff(late_sites,early_sites)),length(setdiff(early_sites,late_sites))))
tab(coverage_changes)
matched <- d[product=="ULP"&month_date %in% as.Date(c("2026-04-01","2026-05-01")),
             .(mean_price=mean(price)),by=month_date]
matched[,population:="All observed sites"]
fixed <- d[product=="ULP"&site %in% common_sites&
             month_date %in% as.Date(c("2026-04-01","2026-05-01")),
           .(mean_price=mean(price)),by=month_date]
fixed[,population:="Sites present in both months"]
tab(rbind(matched,fixed))
```

Site coverage stays at roughly 700–750 ULP sites for most of the period, then
jumps to about 950 in May 2026. Using `intersect()`/`setdiff()`, 748 sites are in
both April and May, 198 appear only in May, and just 3 disappear. The newcomers
are not a random sample: for the shared sites, the mean price falls from 211.6
to 184.9 c/L, but for all sites it only falls to 193.2. So the new sites are
noticeably more expensive, and a naive month-on-month average would understate
the actual price drop. This is one reason I only compare like-for-like periods
and use a relative (same-day, same-region) target later.

These set operations identify changes in observed coverage, not proven business
openings/closures. The common-site check helps separate composition from price
changes but cannot establish causes.

```{r regions}
ggplot(monthly[product=="ULP"],aes(month_date,mean_price,colour=region))+
 geom_line()+facet_wrap(~region,ncol=3)+guides(colour="none")+
 labs(title="Regional ULP trends",x=NULL,y="Price (cents/litre)")
```

All regions follow the same broad up-and-down shape, but the level differs a
lot. Over the whole period Metro is cheapest (about 181 c/L) and Peel and the
South-West are close behind, while the Kimberley averages about 233 c/L, more
than 50 c/L above Perth. Distance from the Kwinana refinery/terminal and
thinner competition are the obvious explanations, although this data alone
cannot prove that. Metro and Peel lines also look much "noisier", which led me
to look at day-of-week patterns.

```{r distributions}
set.seed(params$seed)
plot_sample <- d[sample.int(.N,min(.N,30000))]
ggplot(plot_sample,aes(product,price,fill=product))+geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha=.08)+
 guides(fill="none")+labs(title="Product price distributions",
 subtitle="Seeded plotting sample; summary statistics use all records",
 x=NULL,y="Price (cents/litre)")
```

The boxplots confirm the ordering from the trend chart, but they also show that
diesel has the widest spread (SD about 32 c/L against about 22 for ULP) and the
longest upper tail. Every product has a long upper tail and a fairly tight lower
end. In other words, there is a floor set by wholesale cost and very little room
to go below it, but remote sites can be far above it. This skew is one reason I
used medians rather than means as the reference for "cheap".

```{r ulp-histogram, fig.height=6}
ulp_sample <- plot_sample[product=="ULP"]
ulp_sample[,area_type:=ifelse(region %in% c("METRO","PEEL"),"Metro and Peel","Regional WA")]
hist_plot <- ggplot(ulp_sample,aes(price))+
 geom_histogram(aes(y=after_stat(density)),binwidth=5,fill="#167c80",colour="white")+
 geom_density(colour="#c36b39",linewidth=.8)+facet_wrap(~area_type,ncol=1)+
 labs(title="ULP price: histogram and density",x="Price (c/L)",y="Density")
bar_plot <- ggplot(ulp_sample,aes(y=reorder(region,region,length)))+
 geom_bar(fill="#5479a3")+
 labs(title="ULP records by region (sample)",x="Records",y=NULL)
gridExtra::grid.arrange(hist_plot,bar_plot,ncol=2)
ulp_five <- boxplot.stats(d[product=="ULP",price])$stats
names(ulp_five) <- c("lower whisker","Q1","median","Q3","upper whisker")
tab(t(ulp_five),1)
```

Splitting the ULP histogram by area (with `grid.arrange()` from Lab 2) makes the
skew easier to understand. Metro and Peel have a fairly compact distribution
with a single main peak, while the regional histogram is wider and has a long
right tail that the density curve picks up. The bar chart is a reminder that
most records come from Metro, so a state-wide average is mostly a Perth
average. `boxplot.stats()` gives the five numbers behind the ULP boxplot. The
upper whisker sits at about `r round(ulp_five[5])` c/L, and everything above
that is drawn as an outlier, even though these are real remote prices.

```{r weekday}
weekday_summary <- d[product=="ULP"&date<test_start,.(mean_price=mean(price)),by=.(region,weekday)]
ggplot(weekday_summary,aes(weekday,mean_price,group=region,colour=region))+
 geom_line()+geom_point()+facet_wrap(~region,ncol=3)+guides(colour="none")+
 labs(title="Pre-test ULP weekday associations",subtitle="Associations do not prove a stable price cycle",
 x=NULL,y="Price (cents/litre)")
```

This was the most interesting chart for me. Metro and Peel show a clear weekly
price cycle: Tuesday is the cheapest day (about 169 c/L in Metro) and prices jump
by roughly 27 c/L on Wednesday, then drift down over the following days. The
Wheatbelt shows a weak version of the same pattern, while remote regions like
the Kimberley and Gascoyne are essentially flat (they move by less than 0.5 c/L
across the week). So the weekday effect is real but very local. It matters
mainly in Perth and its surroundings, which is something a model should only
pick up when combined with region.

```{r year-comparison}
# Base-R version of the same summary, using subset() and the native pipe.
annual <- d |>
  subset(product=="ULP" & month<=8,select=c(year,region,price)) |>
  aggregate(price ~ year + region,data=_,FUN=mean) |>
  setNames(c("year","region","mean_price"))
ggplot(annual,aes(factor(year),mean_price,fill=region))+geom_col(position="dodge")+
 labs(title="Comparable January–August periods in every year",
 x="Year (January–August)",y="Price (cents/litre)",fill="Region")
```

Most of the report uses `data.table`, but for this chart and the brand chart
below I used base R `subset()`, `aggregate()` and the native pipe `|>`, as
suggested in the project brief; the results are identical either way.
Comparing the same January–August window each year avoids comparing a full
year with a part year. State-wide ULP averaged about 182.7 c/L in 2023, 189.1
in 2024, 177.9 in 2025 and 193.7 in 2026. So 2025 was the cheapest year and
2026 the most expensive, almost entirely because of the March–April spike. The
ranking of regions barely changes from year to year, with Kimberley always on top
and Metro always near the bottom, which suggests the regional structure is much
more stable than the overall price level.

The exploration moves from overall product differences to within-product region
and weekday patterns. Coverage changes motivate the common-site check; product
differences motivate ULP-only modelling. Test-month plots are descriptive and
are not used to revise the prespecified features or tuning grid below.



## Interpreting the observed patterns

```{r eda-findings, results='asis'}
ranks <- d[product=="ULP" & year==2026 & month<=8,
           .(mean_price=mean(price)),by=region][order(mean_price)]
current <- d[product=="ULP" & year==2026 & month<=8,mean(price)]
previous <- d[product=="ULP" & year==2025 & month<=8,mean(price)]
cat(sprintf("For January to August 2026, the mean ULP notified price is **%.1f c/L**, compared with **%.1f c/L** in the corresponding 2025 months (difference **%+.1f c/L**). These are record-weighted means, so changing site coverage remains a possible contributor.\n\n",
 current,previous,current-previous))
cat(sprintf("Across regions in January to August 2026, %s has the lowest mean ULP price (%.1f c/L), while %s has the highest (%.1f c/L). Regional comparisons should account for coverage and remoteness rather than treating these as brand effects.\n\n",
 ranks$region[1],ranks$mean_price[1],tail(ranks$region,1),tail(ranks$mean_price,1)))
cat(sprintf("Between April and May 2026, observed ULP sites change from **%d to %d**. There are **%d** shared site identifiers. The all-site and shared-site price comparisons above show how sensitive the apparent change is to population composition.\n",
 length(early_sites),length(late_sites),length(common_sites)))
```

```{r brand-comparison}
july_ulp <- subset(d,product=="ULP" & year==2026 & month==7,select=c(brand,price))
brand_ulp <- merge(
  aggregate(price ~ brand,data=july_ulp,FUN=mean) |> setNames(c("brand","mean_price")),
  aggregate(price ~ brand,data=july_ulp,FUN=length) |> setNames(c("brand","records")),
  by="brand")
brand_ulp <- brand_ulp[order(-brand_ulp$records),] |> head(12)
ggplot(brand_ulp,aes(reorder(brand,mean_price),mean_price))+
 geom_col(fill="#167c80")+coord_flip()+
 labs(title="ULP prices for the 12 most-observed brands in July 2026",
 subtitle="Brand differences also reflect geography and station mix",
 x=NULL,y="Mean notified price (c/L)")
```

In July 2026 the cheapest large brands are Atlas, Vibe, United and 7-Eleven
(around 170–175 c/L), while BP (about 199) and Independent (about 216) are the
most expensive. I would be careful with this, though: "Independent" covers many
small rural stations, and BP has a large regional network, so part of this gap
is geography rather than brand pricing policy. Even so, the gap between brands
(more than 40 c/L) is much bigger than the weekday effect, which made brand my
first guess for the strongest single predictor.

## The March 2026 price shock

```{r price-shock}
shock <- d[product=="ULP" & date>=as.Date("2025-09-01")]
shock[,reference:=median(price),by=.(date,region)]
shock_daily <- shock[,.(mean_price=mean(price)),by=date]
top <- max(shock_daily$mean_price)
ggplot(shock_daily,aes(date,mean_price))+
 annotate("rect",xmin=as.Date("2026-03-01"),xmax=as.Date("2026-04-30"),
          ymin=-Inf,ymax=Inf,fill="#c36b39",alpha=.15)+
 annotate("rect",xmin=as.Date("2026-05-01"),xmax=as.Date("2026-07-31"),
          ymin=-Inf,ymax=Inf,fill="#167c80",alpha=.12)+
 annotate("rect",xmin=test_start,xmax=end_date,ymin=-Inf,ymax=Inf,fill="grey50",alpha=.15)+
 geom_line(colour="#173d50",linewidth=.5)+
 annotate("text",x=as.Date("2026-03-31"),y=top+4,label="Price shock\nMar-Apr",size=3.3)+
 annotate("text",x=as.Date("2026-06-15"),y=top+4,label="Recent training\nMay-Jul",size=3.3)+
 annotate("text",x=as.Date("2026-08-16"),y=top+4,label="Test\nAug",size=3.3)+
 labs(title="Daily state-wide ULP average, September 2025 to August 2026",
      subtitle="Shaded windows show the shock, the recent training months and the test month",
      x=NULL,y="Price (c/L)")
shock_month <- shock[,.(mean_price=mean(price),within_day_sd=sd(price-reference),
                        cheap_fraction=mean(price<reference)),by=month_date][order(month_date)]
site_month_rate <- shock[,.(cheap_rate=mean(price<reference)),by=.(site,month_date)]
rate_wide <- dcast(site_month_rate,site~month_date,value.var="cheap_rate")
shock_months <- sort(unique(site_month_rate$month_date))
# Spearman correlation of each site's monthly cheap rate with the previous month.
shock_month[,rank_corr_prev:=c(NA_real_,mapply(function(a,b)
  cor(rate_wide[[as.character(a)]],rate_wide[[as.character(b)]],
      use="complete.obs",method="spearman"),head(shock_months,-1),shock_months[-1]))]
tab(shock_month)
```

From September 2025 to February 2026 the state-wide ULP average sits in a narrow
170–179 c/L band. Then in March 2026 it jumps to about 224 c/L, a rise of
roughly a third in a single month, and diesel peaks even higher in April. News
reports at the time linked this to the war involving Iran and its effect on
crude oil supply ([ABC News, 10 March 2026](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-03-10/why-fuel-prices-are-going-up-australia/106437844)).
The federal government then halved fuel excise for three months from April,
a cut of about 26 c/L ([Reuters, 30 March 2026](https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/australia-halve-tax-petrol-bring-down-costs-wake-iran-war-2026-03-30/)),
which fits the dip from April to June and the rebound once it ran out.
FuelWatch data cannot test these explanations, so I treat them as context, not
as findings. Prices eased back to about 180 by June, then climbed again to about
211 in August, the test month.

**Does the shock make the experiment less objective?** This was my main worry,
so I checked three things in the table above:

1. *The label stays balanced.* Because "cheap" is defined against the same-day,
   same-region median, a price rise that hits every station equally does not
   change anyone's label. The cheap fraction stays between 0.42 and 0.45 in every
   month, including March and April. If I had used a fixed threshold (say,
   "below 180 c/L"), almost every August 2026 record would be "expensive" and
   the experiment would be meaningless.
2. *But the ranking of stations is disturbed.* The rank correlation of each
   site's cheap rate with the previous month is usually around 0.83–0.90, but it
   drops to 0.67 in March and 0.62 in April. During the shock, stations did not
   pass on the increase at the same speed, so which stations count as cheap got
   reshuffled for a while. It recovers to 0.84 by August. This matches reporting
   at the time that the oil shock had reshaped the usual petrol price cycle
   ([ABC News, 31 March 2026](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-03-31/petrol-prices-accc-shape-market/106504912)).
3. *The spread within each day roughly doubles from May.* Within-day SD goes
   from about 10 to 20–24 c/L. Part of this is the 198 extra (mostly regional)
   sites that appear from May, and part is the shock itself.

So the comparison is still fair, since both strategies are tested on exactly
the same August 2026 records with the same label rule. However, the shock is a
genuine distribution shift between the historical Augusts and the 2026 test
month, and I discuss it as part of the training-data comparison rather than
ignoring it.

# Binary classification design

## Target and leakage prevention

For ULP only, **cheap** means strictly below the median price for that date and
region. Ties are **expensive** (at or above the reference), so the classes need
not be balanced. This asks about relative local affordability, not historically
low absolute prices. It dampens common price-level shocks without proving the
absence of structural change.

The contemporaneous regional median is used only to construct the outcome after
prices are observed. It is not known in advance and never enters predictors.
This is a retrospective evaluation of predicting relative affordability from
calendar and site attributes; it does not predict a numerical fuel price.

The candidate predictors are brand, region, weekday, day-of-month and one
engineered feature, **site history** (`site_rate`). Exclude price, median,
price differences, raw site/name/address identifiers, postcode, locality and
area. The latter duplicate geography or are high-cardinality.
Absolute year/date is excluded to avoid unhelpful time extrapolation.

Brand alone is a coarse summary: two BP stations can behave very differently.
Site history is the share of a station's *training* records that were cheap,
smoothed as (cheap + 1) / (records + 2) so that a site seen only a few times is
pulled towards 0.5. This is the Lab 7 `mkPredC()` idea of turning a
categorical variable with thousands of levels into a single probability column.
To avoid leakage: (1) it is learnt only from the training rows of each strategy,
never from the test month; (2) for training rows themselves it is computed
out-of-fold, using five folds of whole dates, so a record's own label never
feeds its own feature; (3) a site that never appears in training gets the
overall training cheap rate.

```{r target}
ulp <- copy(d[product=="ULP"])
ulp[,":="(reference=median(price),reference_n=.N),by=.(date,region)]
ulp[,target:=factor(ifelse(price<reference,"cheap","expensive"),levels=c("expensive","cheap"))]
ulp[,relative_price:=price-reference]
model_data <- ulp[reference_n>=5 & region!="UNKNOWN"]
scope_audit <- data.table(population=c("Clean all-product rows","ULP rows",
                                       "ULP with region reference of >=5 sites"),
                          rows=c(nrow(d),nrow(ulp),nrow(model_data)))
tab(scope_audit)
tab(model_data[,.(n=.N,cheap_fraction=mean(target=="cheap"),
                  ties=mean(price==reference)),by=year])
```

Reference groups with fewer than five sites or missing region are excluded only
from modelling, not removed from cleaned EDA. No target-price imputation occurs.

## How the target relates to the candidate features

Before modelling I looked at the target against each feature with the bar
charts from Lab 4. Only pre-test dates are used, so the August 2026 test month
does not influence the choice of features.

```{r target-eda}
pre_test <- model_data[date<test_start]
top_brands <- pre_test[,.N,by=brand][order(-N)][1:12,brand]
ggplot(pre_test[brand %in% top_brands],
       aes(y=reorder(brand,target=="cheap",FUN=mean),fill=target))+
 geom_bar(position="fill")+geom_vline(xintercept=.5,linetype=2)+
 scale_fill_manual(values=c(expensive="#c36b39",cheap="#167c80"))+
 labs(title="Share of cheap records by brand (filled bar chart)",
      subtitle="Pre-test ULP records; dashed line marks 50%",x="Share",y=NULL,fill="Target")
metro_brands <- c("BP","AMPOL","7-ELEVEN","CALTEX","VIBE","REDDY EXPRESS")
ggplot(pre_test[region=="METRO" & brand %in% metro_brands],aes(weekday,fill=target))+
 geom_bar(position="fill")+facet_wrap(~brand,ncol=3)+
 scale_fill_manual(values=c(expensive="#c36b39",cheap="#167c80"))+
 labs(title="Metro: cheap share by weekday for six large brands",
      subtitle="The weekday effect differs by brand: an interaction a single variable cannot show",
      x=NULL,y="Share",fill="Target")
target_brand <- pre_test[,.N,by=.(brand,region,weekday,target)]
```

The first chart shows why brand is such a strong single predictor. Vibe, United
and Liberty records are cheap about 75–80% of the time, while BP, Caltex and
Independent records are cheap only about 25–28% of the time. Weekday on its own
cannot work in the same way. Because the label compares each station with the
median *of the same day and region*, the cheap share is almost the same on every
weekday by construction (between 0.43 and 0.45).

The second chart shows where weekday still matters. In Metro, 7-Eleven is cheap
on 55% of Tuesdays but only 21% of Wednesdays, which fits it being one of the
first to raise prices at the start of the cycle. BP shows almost the opposite
pattern (11% on Mondays, 36% on Wednesdays), because it raises later and is
briefly cheaper than the stations that have already gone up. Vibe is cheap
almost every day, and Ampol barely changes. So the effect of weekday depends on
the brand. That is an interaction a single-variable model cannot capture, and I
expect models that combine features to gain something over brand alone.

## Training, calibration and final test

- Historical: August 2023, August 2024, August 2025.
- Recent: May, June, July 2026.
- In each source month, a seeded random quarter of the calendar dates forms the
  calibration pool and the remaining dates form the training pool. Splitting by
  whole dates keeps the same regional/day labels in one split, and sampling dates
  across the whole month means calibration covers every part of the month. (An
  earlier version used days 1–24 versus 25–end; calibration then only contained
  days the training bins had never seen, so day-of-month could not be evaluated.)
- Both strategies use the same number of training rows and the same number of
  calibration rows. Each is the size of the smaller pool, so one strategy is
  randomly (seeded) cut down to match the other. The single-variable models,
  Naïve Bayes and the site-history feature use **all** of these training rows.
  The SVM is trained on a seeded subsample of 4,000 of them, because a radial SVM
  with probability estimates scales roughly quadratically with the number of
  rows. A size check later in the report shows what this costs.
- The entire eligible August 2026 test set is held out. Do not retune using it.

Calibration here is a validation set for selecting features/hyperparameters,
not a separate probability-calibration procedure. Historical validation reflects
historical periods, whereas recent validation reflects recent periods: this is
part of the distribution-shift limitation. Sites can recur across periods; the
question concerns future records, not generalisation to entirely unseen sites.

```{r split}
pools <- list(
 Historical=model_data[month==8 & year %in% 2023:2025],
 Recent=model_data[year==2026 & month %in% 5:7])
test <- model_data[date>=test_start & date<=end_date]
if (uniqueN(test$target)!=2L) stop("Test set needs both classes.")
# Pick calibration dates once per pool: a random quarter of the dates in each source month.
cal_dates <- lapply(seq_along(pools),function(i) {
  set.seed(params$seed+i)
  month_dates <- unique(pools[[i]][,.(date,year,month)])
  month_dates[,.(date=date[sample.int(.N,round(.N/4))]),by=.(year,month)]$date
})
n_train <- min(params$train_cap, vapply(seq_along(pools),
  function(i) sum(!pools[[i]]$date %in% cal_dates[[i]]),integer(1)))
n_cal <- min(params$calibration_cap, vapply(seq_along(pools),
  function(i) sum(pools[[i]]$date %in% cal_dates[[i]]),integer(1)))
if (min(n_train,n_cal)<100) stop("Too few rows for the planned experiment.")
splits <- lapply(seq_along(pools),function(i) {
  set.seed(params$seed+i)
  x <- pools[[i]]
  train <- x[!date %in% cal_dates[[i]]]; cal <- x[date %in% cal_dates[[i]]]
  train <- train[sample.int(.N,n_train)]
  cal <- cal[sample.int(.N,n_cal)]
  stopifnot(!length(intersect(train$date,cal$date)),
            max(c(train$date,cal$date))<test_start)
  list(train=train,cal=cal,svm_rows=sort(sample.int(nrow(train),min(params$svm_cap,nrow(train)))))
})
names(splits) <- names(pools)
split_audit <- rbindlist(lapply(names(splits),function(s) {
  rbindlist(lapply(c("train","cal"),function(part) {
    x <- splits[[s]][[part]]
    data.table(strategy=s,split=part,n=nrow(x),first=min(x$date),last=max(x$date),
               cheap_fraction=mean(x$target=="cheap"),sites=uniqueN(x$site))
  }))
}))
tab(split_audit)
tab(test[,.(records=.N,first=min(date),last=max(date),cheap_fraction=mean(target=="cheap"))])
```

## Reusable functions and preprocessing

Rare categorical levels (<20 training observations) and unseen levels map to
OTHER, using training data alone. Conditional-probability baselines and Naïve
Bayes use training-decile bins for day-of-month, following `mkPredN()` from Lab 7,
and the single-variable models are smoothed pivot tables in the spirit of
`mkPredC()`. AUC uses the Lab 7 `calcAUC()` (ROCR), and the Lab 7 `logLikelihood()`
gives the deviance used for variable selection. SVM uses one-hot categorical
columns and training-standardised numeric day and site history. Constant training columns are
removed. No mean, scale, category map or bin boundary is fitted on test data.

```{r model-functions}
# Positive class is cheap. Undefined rates return NA instead of a fictitious zero.
safe_div <- function(a,b) if (b==0) NA_real_ else a/b
# calcAUC() and logLikelihood() follow Lab 7. ytrue is TRUE/FALSE, ypred a probability.
calcAUC <- function(ypred,ytrue) {
  if (length(unique(ytrue))<2) return(NA_real_)
  perf <- ROCR::performance(ROCR::prediction(ypred,ytrue),"auc")
  as.numeric(perf@y.values)
}
logLikelihood <- function(ypred,ytrue) {
  sum(ifelse(ytrue,log(ypred),log(1-ypred)),na.rm=TRUE)
}
auc_cheap <- function(y,p) calcAUC(p,y=="cheap")
metrics <- function(y,p,threshold=.5) {
  if (length(y)!=length(p)||any(!is.finite(p))) stop("Invalid prediction vector.")
  truth <- y=="cheap"; pred <- p>=threshold
  tp<-sum(truth&pred); tn<-sum(!truth&!pred)
  fp<-sum(!truth&pred); fn<-sum(truth&!pred)
  data.table(n=length(y),TP=tp,TN=tn,FP=fp,FN=fn,
    Accuracy=(tp+tn)/length(y),Precision=safe_div(tp,tp+fp),
    Recall=safe_div(tp,tp+fn),Specificity=safe_div(tn,tn+fp),
    F1=safe_div(2*tp,2*tp+fp+fn),
    Balanced_accuracy=mean(c(safe_div(tp,tp+fn),safe_div(tn,tn+fp))),
    AUC=auc_cheap(y,p))
}
# Training-only transformations, including defensible handling of new levels.
fit_preprocessor <- function(x) {
  keep <- lapply(c("brand","region","weekday"),function(nm) {
    freq <- table(as.character(x[[nm]]))
    names(freq)[freq>=20]
  })
  names(keep) <- c("brand","region","weekday")
  # Numeric features: decile cut points (as in mkPredN() from Lab 7) and Z-scaling.
  num <- lapply(intersect(c("day","site_rate"),names(x)),function(nm) {
    v <- x[[nm]]
    list(breaks=unique(c(-Inf,as.numeric(quantile(v,seq(.1,.9,.1))),Inf)),
         centre=mean(v),scale=max(sd(v),1e-8))
  })
  names(num) <- intersect(c("day","site_rate"),names(x))
  list(keep=keep,num=num)
}
transform_categories <- function(x,pp) {
  out <- lapply(names(pp$keep),function(nm) {
    z <- as.character(x[[nm]])
    z[!z %in% pp$keep[[nm]]] <- "OTHER"
    factor(z,levels=unique(c(pp$keep[[nm]],"OTHER")))
  })
  names(out) <- names(pp$keep)
  for (nm in intersect(names(pp$num),names(x))) {
    out[[nm]] <- cut(x[[nm]],breaks=pp$num[[nm]]$breaks,include.lowest=TRUE)
  }
  as.data.frame(out)
}
svm_matrix <- function(x,pp,features) {
  categories <- transform_categories(x,pp)
  pieces <- lapply(features,function(nm) {
    if (nm %in% names(pp$num)) {
      z <- matrix((x[[nm]]-pp$num[[nm]]$centre)/pp$num[[nm]]$scale,ncol=1)
      colnames(z) <- paste0(nm,"_z"); return(z)
    }
    z <- matrix(vapply(levels(categories[[nm]]),function(lv)
      as.numeric(categories[[nm]]==lv),numeric(nrow(x))),nrow=nrow(x))
    colnames(z)<-paste(nm,levels(categories[[nm]]),sep="_")
    z
  })
  do.call(cbind,pieces)
}
# Laplace-smoothed pivot-table conditional probabilities; unknowns use prior.
fit_single <- function(x,y) {
  counts <- data.table(level=as.character(x),positive=as.integer(y=="cheap"))[
    ,.(p=(sum(positive)+1)/(.N+2)),by=level]
  list(p=setNames(counts$p,counts$level),prior=mean(y=="cheap"))
}
predict_single <- function(model,x) {
  p <- unname(model$p[as.character(x)])
  p[is.na(p)]<-model$prior
  p
}
# Site history: smoothed share of cheap records per site, learnt from training rows only.
# Sites never seen in training get the training prior.
site_rate_lookup <- function(x,history,prior) {
  counts <- history[,.(k=sum(target=="cheap"),n=.N),by=site]
  m <- counts[match(x$site,counts$site)]
  ifelse(is.na(m$n),prior,(m$k+1)/(m$n+2))
}
# Training rows get out-of-fold values (folds of whole dates), so a row's own label
# never feeds its own feature; calibration and test rows use all training rows.
encode_site <- function(train,others,seed,folds=5) {
  if (!all(c("site","date","target") %in% names(train))) stop("encode_site needs site, date, target.")
  prior <- mean(train$target=="cheap")
  set.seed(seed)
  dates <- sort(unique(train$date))
  fold_of_date <- sample(rep_len(seq_len(folds),length(dates)))
  fold <- fold_of_date[match(train$date,dates)]
  train_rate <- numeric(nrow(train))
  for (k in seq_len(folds)) {
    idx <- which(fold==k)
    train_rate[idx] <- site_rate_lookup(train[idx],train[-idx],prior)
  }
  list(train=train_rate,others=lapply(others,site_rate_lookup,history=train,prior=prior))
}
# One fitted NB/SVM object; it owns the transformation fitted on its training data.
fit_classifier <- function(train,pp,features,method,cost=1,gamma=NULL) {
  if (uniqueN(train$target)!=2) stop("Both target classes needed.")
  if (method=="NB") {
    xx <- transform_categories(train,pp)[,features,drop=FALSE]
    fit <- e1071::naiveBayes(x=xx,y=train$target,laplace=1)
    return(structure(list(fit=fit,pp=pp,features=features,method=method),
                     class="fuel_classifier"))
  }
  xx <- svm_matrix(train,pp,features)
  active <- apply(xx,2,sd)>1e-8
  xx <- xx[,active,drop=FALSE]
  if (!ncol(xx)) stop("No varying SVM features.")
  if (is.null(gamma)) gamma <- 1/ncol(xx)
  fit <- e1071::svm(x=xx,y=train$target,kernel="radial",cost=cost,
                     gamma=gamma,scale=FALSE,probability=TRUE,cachesize=200)
  structure(list(fit=fit,pp=pp,features=features,method=method,active=active),
            class="fuel_classifier")
}
predict_classifier <- function(model,x) {
  if (model$method=="NB") {
    xx <- transform_categories(x,model$pp)[,model$features,drop=FALSE]
    return(as.numeric(predict(model$fit,xx,type="raw")[,"cheap"]))
  }
  xx <- svm_matrix(x,model$pp,model$features)[,model$active,drop=FALSE]
  ans <- predict(model$fit,xx,probability=TRUE)
  as.numeric(attr(ans,"probabilities")[,"cheap"])
}
```

## Feature selection and tuning

The primary selection metric is calibration AUC: ranking relatively cheap
records matters, and AUC is threshold-independent. Report F1 and balanced
accuracy at the fixed 0.5 probability cutoff alongside accuracy. A null model
predicts the majority class; its constant score has AUC 0.5.

For each strategy, rank five single-variable models on calibration AUC, and also
compute each one's deviance reduction against the null model on calibration,
`2 × (logLik(model) − logLik(null))`, as in Lab 7. Three candidate feature sets
are compared in NB and SVM: the top two by AUC, all five, and the Lab 7 rule,
i.e. every variable whose deviance reduction is at least 10 (duplicate sets are
dropped). Tune SVM cost (0.5, 2) and
gamma (1/p, 2/p), with p the number of active input columns. Select using
calibration AUC only. The modest fixed grid and the 4,000-row SVM subsample are
computational trade-offs, not claims of globally optimal tuning. The main models
keep the natural class balance; two imbalance treatments are compared separately
after the main results.

```{r training}
min_drop <- 10
results <- list(); single_tables <- list(); tune_tables <- list()
predictions <- list(); roc_tables <- list(); selected <- list(); fitted_models <- list()
encoded <- list()
for (strategy in names(splits)) {
  train <- copy(splits[[strategy]]$train)
  cal <- copy(splits[[strategy]]$cal)
  test_s <- copy(test)
  enc <- encode_site(train,list(cal=cal,test=test_s),seed=params$seed+50)
  train[,site_rate:=enc$train]; cal[,site_rate:=enc$others$cal]; test_s[,site_rate:=enc$others$test]
  svm_train <- train[splits[[strategy]]$svm_rows]
  encoded[[strategy]] <- list(train=train,cal=cal,test=test_s,svm_train=svm_train)
  pp <- fit_preprocessor(train)
  trcat <- transform_categories(train,pp)
  cacat <- transform_categories(cal,pp)
  features <- c("brand","region","weekday","day","site_rate")
  singles <- setNames(lapply(features,function(f) fit_single(trcat[[f]],train$target)),features)
  # Null-model log likelihood on calibration, as in Lab 7.
  logNull <- logLikelihood(mean(cal$target=="cheap"),cal$target=="cheap")
  ranking <- rbindlist(lapply(features,function(f) {
    p <- predict_single(singles[[f]],cacat[[f]])
    data.table(feature=f,AUC=auc_cheap(cal$target,p),
               deviance_reduction=2*(logLikelihood(p,cal$target=="cheap")-logNull))
  }))
  setorder(ranking,-AUC,feature)
  ranking[,strategy:=strategy]
  single_tables[[strategy]] <- ranking
  best_single <- ranking$feature[1]
  dev_selected <- ranking[deviance_reduction>=min_drop,feature]
  if (!length(dev_selected)) dev_selected <- best_single
  feature_sets <- list(Top2=ranking$feature[1:2],All=features,DevDrop=dev_selected)
  feature_sets <- feature_sets[!duplicated(lapply(feature_sets,sort))]
  candidates <- list(); score_rows <- list(); counter <- 0L
  for (set_name in names(feature_sets)) {
    fs <- feature_sets[[set_name]]
    counter <- counter+1L
    nb <- fit_classifier(train,pp,fs,"NB")
    candidates[[counter]] <- nb
    score_rows[[counter]] <- data.table(id=counter,method="NB",feature_set=set_name,
      features=paste(fs,collapse=" + "),cost=NA_real_,gamma=NA_real_,
      AUC=auc_cheap(cal$target,predict_classifier(nb,cal)))
    xx <- svm_matrix(svm_train,pp,fs)
    p <- sum(apply(xx,2,sd)>1e-8)
    for (cost in c(.5,2)) for (mult in c(1,2)) {
      counter <- counter+1L
      set.seed(params$seed+counter)
      svm <- fit_classifier(svm_train,pp,fs,"SVM",cost=cost,gamma=mult/p)
      candidates[[counter]] <- svm
      score_rows[[counter]] <- data.table(id=counter,method="SVM",feature_set=set_name,
        features=paste(fs,collapse=" + "),cost=cost,gamma=mult/p,
        AUC=auc_cheap(cal$target,predict_classifier(svm,cal)))
    }
  }
  tuning <- rbindlist(score_rows)
  tuning[,strategy:=strategy]
  tune_tables[[strategy]] <- tuning
  nb_id <- tuning[method=="NB"][which.max(AUC),id]
  svm_id <- tuning[method=="SVM"][which.max(AUC),id]
  winners <- candidates[c(nb_id,svm_id)]
  names(winners) <- c("NB","SVM")
  selected[[strategy]] <- tuning[id %in% c(nb_id,svm_id)]
  fitted_models[[strategy]] <- list(models=winners,singles=singles,best_single=best_single,pp=pp)
  for (split_name in c("Train","Calibration","Test")) {
    x <- switch(split_name,Train=train,Calibration=cal,Test=test_s)
    probs <- list(Null=rep(mean(train$target=="cheap"),nrow(x)),
      Single=predict_single(singles[[best_single]],transform_categories(x,pp)[[best_single]]),
      NB=predict_classifier(winners$NB,x),SVM=predict_classifier(winners$SVM,x))
    for (method in names(probs)) {
      p_hat <- probs[[method]]
      met <- metrics(x$target,p_hat)
      met[,":="(strategy=strategy,split=split_name,model=method)]
      results[[length(results)+1L]] <- met
      if (split_name=="Test") {
        predictions[[paste(strategy,method)]] <- data.table(strategy=strategy,model=method,
          row=seq_len(nrow(x)),date=x$date,site=x$site,truth=x$target,probability=p_hat)
        ro <- pROC::roc(x$target,p_hat,levels=c("expensive","cheap"),direction="<",quiet=TRUE)
        roc_tables[[paste(strategy,method)]] <- data.table(strategy=strategy,model=method,
          FPR=1-ro$specificities,TPR=ro$sensitivities)
      }
    }
  }
}
evaluation <- rbindlist(results)
single_scores <- rbindlist(single_tables)
tuning_scores <- rbindlist(tune_tables)
selected_models <- rbindlist(selected)
test_predictions <- rbindlist(predictions)
roc_data <- rbindlist(roc_tables)
tab(single_scores)
tab(selected_models[,.(strategy,method,feature_set,features,cost,gamma,calibration_AUC=AUC)])
```

```{r model-evaluation}
tab(evaluation[,.(strategy,split,model,n,Accuracy,Precision,Recall,Specificity,F1,Balanced_accuracy,AUC)])
tab(evaluation[split=="Test",.(strategy,model,TP,FP,FN,TN)])
ggplot(roc_data,aes(FPR,TPR,colour=model)) + geom_line(linewidth=.8) +
 geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,linetype=2,colour="grey60")+
 facet_wrap(~strategy)+coord_equal()+
 labs(title="Final August 2026 ROC curves",subtitle="Cheap is the positive class",
      x="False-positive rate",y="True-positive rate",colour="Model")
```

```{r feature-comparison}
ggplot(tuning_scores,aes(feature_set,AUC,colour=method))+
 geom_point(position=position_jitter(width=.08,height=0,seed=params$seed),size=2)+
 facet_wrap(~strategy)+labs(title="Feature combinations: calibration performance",
 x="Feature subset",y="Calibration AUC")
```

## Class imbalance treatment

About 45% of records are cheap, so the imbalance is mild, but it still matters at
the 0.5 cut-off: models lean towards "expensive" and miss cheap records. I tried
two treatments. Both are decided without looking at the test month:

1. **Random oversampling** of cheap records in the training rows only, so that
   the classes are 50/50. Calibration and test are never resampled. For SVM the
   training size is kept at the same 4,000 rows.
2. **Moving the cut-off.** Keep the model, but instead of 0.5 use the probability
   threshold that maximises F1 on the calibration set.

```{r imbalance}
best_threshold <- function(y,p) {
  grid <- seq(.2,.8,by=.01)
  f1 <- vapply(grid,function(t) metrics(y,p,t)$F1,numeric(1))
  grid[which.max(f1)]
}
oversample <- function(x,seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  cheap <- x[target=="cheap"]; dear <- x[target=="expensive"]
  rbind(dear,cheap[sample.int(.N,nrow(dear),replace=TRUE)])
}
imbalance_rows <- list()
for (strategy in names(encoded)) {
  e <- encoded[[strategy]]; models <- fitted_models[[strategy]]$models
  for (m in c("NB","SVM")) {
    base <- models[[m]]
    p_cal <- predict_classifier(base,e$cal); p_test <- predict_classifier(base,e$test)
    t_star <- best_threshold(e$cal$target,p_cal)
    src <- if (m=="SVM") e$svm_train else e$train
    os <- oversample(src,params$seed+70)
    if (m=="SVM") os <- os[sample.int(.N,nrow(src))]
    refit <- fit_classifier(os,base$pp,base$features,m,
                            cost=if (m=="SVM") base$fit$cost else 1,
                            gamma=if (m=="SVM") base$fit$gamma else NULL)
    p_os <- predict_classifier(refit,e$test)
    imbalance_rows[[length(imbalance_rows)+1L]] <- rbind(
      metrics(e$test$target,p_test)[,treatment:="None (cut-off 0.5)"],
      metrics(e$test$target,p_test,t_star)[,treatment:=sprintf("Cut-off tuned on calibration (%.2f)",t_star)],
      metrics(e$test$target,p_os)[,treatment:="Oversampled training (cut-off 0.5)"]
    )[,":="(strategy=strategy,model=m)]
  }
}
imbalance <- rbindlist(imbalance_rows)
tab(imbalance[,.(strategy,model,treatment,Precision,Recall,F1,Balanced_accuracy,AUC)])
imbalance_long <- melt(imbalance[,.(strategy,model,treatment=sub(" \\(.*","",treatment),
                                    Precision,Recall,F1)],
                       id.vars=c("strategy","model","treatment"))
ggplot(imbalance_long,aes(variable,value,fill=treatment))+geom_col(position="dodge")+
 facet_grid(model~strategy)+coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,1))+
 scale_fill_manual(values=c("#9fb8c2","#167c80","#c36b39"))+
 labs(title="Imbalance treatments on the August 2026 test",
      subtitle="Treatments trade precision for recall; AUC (ranking) is almost unchanged",
      x=NULL,y="Score",fill=NULL)
```

Moving the cut-off has the bigger effect. The F1-best threshold found on
calibration is well below 0.5 (0.26–0.33), and on the test it raises F1 in all
four cases, for example from 0.737 to 0.746 for the recent SVM and from 0.613 to
0.643 for the historical SVM. It does this by finding many more cheap records
(recall up by 0.06–0.25) while recommending more stations that turn out to be
expensive (precision down by 0.05–0.17). For the historical models the drop in
precision is large, and balanced accuracy actually falls (0.684 to 0.639 for
SVM), so the cut-off that suited past Augusts is too aggressive for 2026.
Oversampling gives smaller and more even gains (F1 up by 0.005–0.016). As
expected, AUC hardly changes with either treatment, because neither changes how
the model *ranks* stations. So the choice depends on the user: someone who
wants to find as many cheap stations as possible should use a lower cut-off;
someone who hates driving to an expensive one should keep 0.5.

## Does training on more rows help?

The SVM only sees 4,000 training rows. To check what this costs, I refitted the
selected recent-strategy NB and SVM on growing random subsets of the training
rows and scored them on the **calibration** set, so the test month stays untouched.
The SVM stops at 8,000 rows because fitting time grows quickly.

```{r training-size}
e <- encoded$Recent; base <- fitted_models$Recent$models
set.seed(params$seed+80)
row_order <- sample.int(nrow(e$train))
size_grid <- sort(unique(pmin(c(1000,2000,4000,8000,nrow(e$train)),nrow(e$train))))
size_scores <- rbindlist(lapply(size_grid,function(n) {
  sub <- e$train[row_order[seq_len(n)]]
  nb <- fit_classifier(sub,base$NB$pp,base$NB$features,"NB")
  out <- data.table(rows=n,model="NB",calibration_AUC=auc_cheap(e$cal$target,predict_classifier(nb,e$cal)),
                    fit_seconds=NA_real_)
  if (n<=8000) {
    t0 <- Sys.time()
    svm <- fit_classifier(sub,base$SVM$pp,base$SVM$features,"SVM",
                          cost=base$SVM$fit$cost,gamma=base$SVM$fit$gamma)
    secs <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(),t0,units="secs"))
    out <- rbind(out,data.table(rows=n,model="SVM",
      calibration_AUC=auc_cheap(e$cal$target,predict_classifier(svm,e$cal)),fit_seconds=secs))
  }
  out
}))
tab(size_scores)
ggplot(size_scores,aes(rows,calibration_AUC,colour=model))+geom_line()+geom_point(size=2)+
 scale_x_log10(labels=scales::comma)+
 labs(title="Calibration AUC against number of training rows (recent strategy)",
      x="Training rows (log scale)",y="Calibration AUC",colour="Model")
```

The curve is almost flat. NB improves only from 0.907 with 1,000 rows to 0.914
with all 49,448, and the SVM is already at 0.914 with 1,000 rows. It peaks at
4,000 rows (0.917) and is slightly lower at 8,000 (0.915), while fitting time
roughly quadruples each time the rows double (last column). So training the SVM on 4,000 rows costs
essentially nothing in accuracy here. Most of the information is in the site
history, which is computed from all training rows anyway.

### Reading the results

```{r findings, results='asis'}
for (s in names(splits)) {
  z <- evaluation[strategy==s & split=="Test"]
  baseline <- max(z[model %in% c("Null","Single"),AUC])
  cat(sprintf("\n**%s training:** null AUC %.3f; best single-variable AUC %.3f; NB %.3f; SVM %.3f.\n\n",
      s,z[model=="Null",AUC],z[model=="Single",AUC],z[model=="NB",AUC],z[model=="SVM",AUC]))
  for (m in c("NB","SVM")) {
    delta <- z[model==m,AUC]-baseline
    cat(sprintf("- %s %s the stronger baseline by %.3f AUC on this test month.\n",
                m,if(delta>0) "exceeds" else "does not exceed",
                abs(delta)))
  }
}
```

Training performance is descriptive, not independent evidence. Calibration scores
are optimistic after selecting their maximum; the final test provides the
held-out comparison. Increased complexity is supported only if it improves on
both baselines in metrics relevant to the question. An AUC advantage does not
guarantee better precision or recall at 0.5.

**My reading of the classification results.**

*The null model shows why accuracy is not enough.* It always predicts
"expensive" and still gets 55% accuracy on August 2026, simply because 55% of
records are expensive. But it never finds a single cheap station (recall 0,
F1 0, AUC 0.5). Any model I keep has to do clearly better than this on recall,
F1 and AUC, not just on accuracy.

*Feature selection.* Both of the measures from Lab 7 now put the new
site-history feature far ahead of everything else. Its calibration AUC is 0.85
(historical) and 0.91 (recent), with deviance reductions of about 7,800 and
11,100. Brand comes second (AUC 0.71 and 0.76; deviance reduction about 3,100
and 4,000). In other words, *which station it is* says much more than *which
brand it flies*: two BP stations can behave very differently, and the site
feature sees that, while brand cannot. Weekday and day-of-month are close to
useless on their own: AUC is about 0.51, and the deviance reduction is small or
even negative. For day-of-month in the historical strategy, a negative value
means that the ten decile bins fitted on training make the calibration
predictions slightly *worse* than the null model, which is a small but clear
sign of overfitting. As the target EDA showed, the label is balanced within
every day and region, so weekday can only help through its interaction with
brand.

Region now passes the Lab 7 threshold in both strategies (deviance reduction
115 and 45, above `minDrop = 10`) even though its AUC is only 0.51–0.53.
Deviance rewards probabilities that are well calibrated, whereas AUC only
measures ranking, so a variable can shift the predicted probabilities in the
right direction without helping much to rank stations. So the deviance rule
picks site history + brand + region in both strategies.

The three feature sets end up very close. For SVM, the best calibration AUC is
0.857 with all five features against 0.854 for the top two (historical), and
0.9183 against 0.9182 (recent). For NB the difference is in the fourth decimal
place. All five features won narrowly in every case, so that is what was
selected. Once site history is in the model, brand, weekday and day add very
little on top.

*Is the extra complexity worth it?* Only barely, in both strategies:

- With **historical** training, the site-history lookup alone reaches a test
  AUC of 0.728. NB (0.722) does slightly worse, and SVM (0.731) is only 0.004
  better. F1 is about 0.61 for all three.
- With **recent** training, the picture is the same at a higher level: site
  history alone 0.836, NB 0.837, SVM 0.839. SVM has the best F1 (0.737 vs
  0.730) and recall (0.70 vs 0.69), with similar precision (about 0.78).

So by the rule I set at the start, the more complex models are not really
justified: a lookup table of each station's past cheap rate does almost as
well. I still find it a useful result. It means that the main information is
"this station is usually cheap", and that NB and SVM cannot find much extra
structure in brand and calendar once they know that.

Compared with the earlier version of this analysis (brand, region, weekday and
day only), adding site history raised the recent-strategy SVM test AUC from
about 0.73 to 0.84 and its F1 from about 0.62 to 0.74.

Training and calibration AUC (about 0.86 historical, 0.91 recent) are higher
than test AUC, and the gap is much bigger for the historical strategy (0.86 on
calibration against 0.73 on the test). The historical calibration days are
themselves from past Augusts, so they share the training distribution and could
not warn me about the shift to 2026. This is a nice example of why a validation
set only protects you if it looks like the data you will actually predict.

## Explaining individual SVM predictions with LIME

An AUC tells me how well the SVM ranks stations, but not *why* it calls a
particular station cheap. Following Lab 6, I used LIME as an automated sanity
check on the selected recent-strategy SVM. LIME does not know our model class
out of the box, so the two methods it needs (`model_type` and `predict_model`)
are registered for it. Day-of-month is binned into quartiles for the explanation.

```{r lime-explain, fig.height=7, warning=FALSE}
registerS3method("model_type","fuel_classifier",
                 function(x,...) "classification",envir=asNamespace("lime"))
registerS3method("predict_model","fuel_classifier",function(x,newdata,type,...) {
  p <- predict_classifier(x,as.data.table(newdata))
  data.frame(expensive=1-p,cheap=p)
},envir=asNamespace("lime"))
lime_cols <- fitted_models$Recent$models$SVM$features
lime_train <- as.data.frame(encoded$Recent$svm_train[,..lime_cols])
char_cols <- intersect(c("brand","region"),lime_cols)
for (nm in char_cols) lime_train[[nm]] <- factor(lime_train[[nm]])
explainer <- lime::lime(lime_train,model=fitted_models$Recent$models$SVM,
                        bin_continuous=TRUE,n_bins=4)
eligible <- encoded$Recent$test
for (nm in char_cols) eligible <- eligible[get(nm) %in% levels(lime_train[[nm]])]
set.seed(params$seed)
pick <- function(rows) rows[sample.int(length(rows),1)]
cases <- c(pick(eligible[,which(region=="METRO" & target=="cheap")]),
           pick(eligible[,which(region=="METRO" & target=="expensive")]),
           pick(eligible[,which(region!="METRO" & target=="cheap")]),
           pick(eligible[,which(region!="METRO" & target=="expensive")]))
lime_cases <- as.data.frame(eligible[cases,..lime_cols])
for (nm in char_cols) lime_cases[[nm]] <- factor(lime_cases[[nm]],levels=levels(lime_train[[nm]]))
tab(cbind(case=1:4,eligible[cases,.(brand,region,weekday,day,site_rate=round(site_rate,2),target)]))
explanation <- lime::explain(lime_cases,explainer,n_labels=1,n_features=4)
lime::plot_features(explanation)
lime_summary <- as.data.table(explanation)[order(case,-abs(feature_weight)),
  .(predicted=label[1],probability=label_prob[1],top_feature=feature_desc[1],
    top_weight=feature_weight[1],fit=model_r2[1]),by=case]
tab(lime_summary)
fwrite(as.data.table(explanation)[,.(case,label,label_prob,feature_desc,feature_weight,model_r2)],
       "outputs/lime_explanations.csv")
```

```{r lime-findings, results='asis'}
site_top <- sum(grepl("site_rate",lime_summary$top_feature))
correct <- sum(lime_summary$predicted==as.character(eligible[cases,target]))
cat(sprintf("The SVM labels **%d of the 4** cases correctly. In **%d of the 4** cases, the feature with the largest LIME weight is site history.\n\n",
            correct,site_top))
```

This is the kind of sanity check Lab 6 describes with the wolf-and-husky
example. I wanted to make sure the SVM is not relying on something meaningless,
such as a particular day-of-month bin. It is not. Site history has by far the
largest weight in every case (about 0.44–0.57). Everything else (region, brand,
weekday, day) is below 0.09, and usually below 0.03. This fits the
single-variable results: once the model knows a station's track record, the
other features barely move the prediction.

Case 3 is a good example of what the new feature fixes. It is an Independent
station in the Wheatbelt that was cheap that day. Most Independents *are*
expensive (only about a quarter of their records are cheap), and in the earlier
brand-only version of this analysis the SVM got exactly this kind of station
wrong. This station, however, was cheap in 83% of its training records, so the
SVM now calls it cheap with probability 0.87, and brand only pushes slightly the
other way. The explanation fit (R² about 0.38–0.57) is moderate, because the
local linear surrogate is only a rough approximation of the radial kernel. So I
read the bars as "which way each feature pushes this prediction", not as exact
effects.

# Which training data works better?

Both strategies use identical sample sizes, outcome rules, feature candidates,
tuning grids and final test rows. Their category composition and time period may
still differ. Compare price distributions as context, although prices are not
predictors. A general price-level shock can affect historical-threshold labels
more strongly than the local-relative label used here.

```{r distribution-shift}
shift <- rbindlist(lapply(names(pools),function(s) {
  pools[[s]][,.(period=s,records=.N,sites=uniqueN(site),mean_price=mean(price),
               sd_price=sd(price),cheap_fraction=mean(target=="cheap"))]
}))
shift <- rbind(shift,test[,.(period="August 2026 test",records=.N,sites=uniqueN(site),
                mean_price=mean(price),sd_price=sd(price),cheap_fraction=mean(target=="cheap"))])
tab(shift)
unseen <- rbindlist(lapply(names(splits),function(s) {
  data.table(strategy=s,new_site_fraction=mean(!test$site %in% splits[[s]]$train$site),
             new_brand_fraction=mean(!test$brand %in% splits[[s]]$train$brand))
}))
tab(unseen)
```

## Paired uncertainty and common-site sensitivity

Resample whole test dates jointly for both strategies, not individual rows,
to preserve within-day dependence. The percentile interval below is descriptive:
31 dates are few, consecutive days may be autocorrelated, and training uncertainty
is not included. It is not a definitive causal or significance claim.

```{r paired-bootstrap}
set.seed(params$seed+100)
date_indices <- split(seq_len(nrow(test)),test$date)
bootstrap <- rbindlist(lapply(c("NB","SVM"),function(m) {
  a <- test_predictions[strategy=="Historical"&model==m][order(row)]$probability
  b <- test_predictions[strategy=="Recent"&model==m][order(row)]$probability
  delta <- replicate(params$bootstrap_reps,{
    sampled <- sample.int(length(date_indices),length(date_indices),replace=TRUE)
    ix <- unlist(date_indices[sampled],use.names=FALSE)
    auc_cheap(test$target[ix],b[ix])-auc_cheap(test$target[ix],a[ix])
  })
  data.table(model=m,recent_minus_historical=auc_cheap(test$target,b)-auc_cheap(test$target,a),
             lower=quantile(delta,.025,na.rm=TRUE),upper=quantile(delta,.975,na.rm=TRUE))
}))
tab(bootstrap)
shared_training_sites <- intersect(splits$Historical$train$site,splits$Recent$train$site)
common_test <- test$site %in% shared_training_sites
common_metrics <- test_predictions[site %in% shared_training_sites,
   as.list(metrics(truth,probability)),by=.(strategy,model)]
tab(common_metrics[,.(strategy,model,n,AUC,F1,Balanced_accuracy)])
```

The common-site sensitivity keeps the original region/day target definitions.
Differences from the full test may reflect site coverage. It is a secondary
analysis, not a reason to retune on the test set. A stronger study would repeat
the locked protocol on additional target months; one August cannot establish a
universal winner or stable seasonality across years.

## What "more accurate" means here, and why recent data wins

My prediction question is: *on a given day in August 2026, can I tell, before
looking at the price, whether a ULP station will be cheaper than the local
median?* So "more accurate" means **higher test AUC on August 2026**, i.e. better
at ranking the cheap stations above the expensive ones. F1 and recall are my
secondary measures, because a driver mainly cares about finding cheap stations.
Accuracy alone is not useful here, as the null model already shows.

On that definition, recent training wins clearly. Test AUC is higher by about
0.11 for both NB and SVM, and the date-bootstrap intervals (roughly 0.10–0.13
and 0.10–0.12) are far above zero. With the site-history feature the gap is
about twice as big as in the earlier brand-only version (0.04–0.06), because
this feature depends directly on *which* stations the training data has seen
and how they behaved. The same pattern holds when I restrict the test to sites
that appear in both training sets (SVM 0.840 vs 0.774), so it is not only about
the recent strategy having seen more of the test sites.

Why? The tables above suggest three reasons, all forms of distribution shift:

1. **Site coverage.** About 24% of August 2026 test records come from sites that
   never appear in the historical training data, against only 0.3% for the
   recent strategy. The ~200 sites added in May 2026 are simply invisible to a
   model trained on 2023–2025, and for them site history falls back to the
   overall average. Restricting to shared sites closes the SVM gap from 0.108 to
   0.066 AUC, so coverage explains roughly 40% of it.
2. **The market changed after the shock.** The month-to-month stability of which
   stations are cheap dropped sharply in March–April 2026. A station's track
   record in August 2024 is a weaker guide to August 2026 than its record in
   July 2026.
3. **The weekly cycle weakened.** Before March 2026 the Metro Tuesday-to-Wednesday
   jump was about 30 c/L. From March 2026 onwards it is only about 11–14 c/L.
   Historical Augusts teach the model a cycle that is much weaker in the test
   month.

The argument *for* historical Augusts would be seasonality: perhaps August has
its own month-specific pattern. I do not see much evidence for that. Day-of-month
has no predictive value in either strategy, and the regional/brand ordering is
stable across the year. For a relative label like this one, how recent the data
is matters much more than matching the calendar month. I would expect the
answer to be different for a fixed-price threshold (for example, predicting
whether a price is below 180 c/L), where seasonal price levels would matter more.
The caveat is that this is one test month just after an unusual shock, so I
would not claim that recent data always wins.

# Clustering site price profiles

Clustering uses ULP observations in **May–July 2026**, a common pre-test window.
Sites require at least 60 observed days; this is a reliability subset, not a
cleaning deletion. Features describe average deviation from the regional/day
median, price standard deviation, average absolute change between consecutive
observed calendar days, and the fraction of consecutive-day price increases.
Missing gaps are not treated as one-day changes.

Features are Z-standardised so cents and proportions do not dominate merely
because of units. Near-zero-variance columns and features correlated above
|0.90| with an already retained feature are removed. K-means uses squared
Euclidean distances; silhouette uses Euclidean distances on the same scaled
features. Compare k=2–6 using silhouette and within-cluster sum of squares.

```{r clustering}
site_daily <- copy(ulp[year==2026 & month %in% 5:7])
setorder(site_daily,site,date)
site_daily[,change:=ifelse(as.integer(date-shift(date))==1,price-shift(price),NA_real_),by=site]
profiles <- site_daily[,.(days=.N,site_name=site_name[.N],brand=brand[.N],region=region[.N],
  mean_price=mean(price),relative_mean=mean(relative_price),price_sd=sd(price),
  mean_abs_change=mean(abs(change),na.rm=TRUE),increase_rate=mean(change>0,na.rm=TRUE)),by=site]
cluster_scope <- data.table(population=c("ULP sites in May–July","Sites with >=60 days"),
                            sites=c(nrow(profiles),sum(profiles$days>=60)))
profiles <- profiles[days>=60]
candidate_features <- c("relative_mean","price_sd","mean_abs_change","increase_rate")
valid <- complete.cases(profiles[,..candidate_features])
cluster_scope <- rbind(cluster_scope,data.table(population="Complete numeric profiles",sites=sum(valid)))
profiles <- profiles[valid]
if (nrow(profiles)<20) stop("Too few sites for clustering.")
candidate_features <- candidate_features[vapply(profiles[,..candidate_features],sd,numeric(1))>1e-8]
correlations <- cor(profiles[,..candidate_features])
cluster_features <- character()
for (f in candidate_features) {
  if (!length(cluster_features)||all(abs(correlations[f,cluster_features])<=.90)) {
    cluster_features<-c(cluster_features,f)
  }
}
scaled <- scale(as.matrix(profiles[,..cluster_features]))
distance <- dist(scaled,method="euclidean")
ks <- 2:min(6,nrow(profiles)-1)
cluster_fits <- list()
cluster_scores <- rbindlist(lapply(ks,function(k) {
  set.seed(params$seed+k)
  km <- kmeans(scaled,centers=k,nstart=30,iter.max=100)
  cluster_fits[[as.character(k)]] <<- km
  sil <- cluster::silhouette(km$cluster,distance)
  data.table(k=k,WSS=km$tot.withinss,silhouette=mean(sil[,3]),
             smallest_cluster=min(table(km$cluster)))
}))
best_k <- cluster_scores[which.max(silhouette),k]
profiles[,cluster:=factor(cluster_fits[[as.character(best_k)]]$cluster)]
pca <- prcomp(scaled,center=FALSE,scale.=FALSE)
profiles[,":="(PC1=pca$x[,1],PC2=pca$x[,2])]
cluster_centres <- profiles[,lapply(.SD,mean),by=cluster,
  .SDcols=c("mean_price",candidate_features)]
cluster_centres <- merge(cluster_centres,profiles[,.N,by=cluster],by="cluster")
tab(cluster_scope)
tab(as.data.table(correlations,keep.rownames="feature"))
cat("Retained features:",paste(cluster_features,collapse=", "))
tab(cluster_scores)
tab(cluster_centres)
```

Before clustering I looked at how the four site features relate to each other,
using the pairwise scatter grid and a smoothed scatter plot from Lab 4.

```{r profile-pairs, fig.height=7}
area_colour <- ifelse(profiles$region %in% c("METRO","PEEL"),"#167c80","#c36b39")
pairs(profiles[,..candidate_features],col=area_colour,pch=20,cex=.6,
      main="Site profile features (teal = Metro/Peel, orange = regional)")
profiles[,area_type:=ifelse(region %in% c("METRO","PEEL"),"Metro and Peel","Regional WA")]
ggplot(profiles,aes(mean_abs_change,increase_rate,colour=area_type))+
 geom_point(alpha=.5)+geom_smooth(method="loess",se=FALSE)+
 labs(title="Daily price movement vs share of days with a price rise",
      x="Mean absolute day-to-day change (c/L)",y="Share of days with a rise",colour=NULL)
```

The pairs plot shows two clear things. First, the remote sites stand far apart
on `relative_mean`, which is why I expect them to form their own group. Second,
Metro/Peel sites (teal) and regional sites (orange) largely separate on the two
movement features. The typical regional site moves by about 0.7 c/L a day and
raises its price on about 5% of days, while the typical Metro site moves by about
2.8 c/L and raises on about 18% of days. The smoothed scatter plot adds a less
obvious pattern. Among Metro sites, those with moderate moves (1–2 c/L) raise
prices most often (about 25% of days), while the big cyclers (6+ c/L moves)
raise less often (about 16%) but by much more. This is what a price cycle looks
like at site level: one sharp jump followed by several small cuts. Since the
two movement features are related but clearly not the same thing, it makes
sense that the correlation filter kept both.

```{r cluster-plots}
score_long <- melt(cluster_scores,id.vars="k",measure.vars=c("WSS","silhouette"))
ggplot(score_long,aes(k,value))+geom_line(colour="#167c80")+geom_point(size=2)+
 facet_wrap(~variable,scales="free_y")+
 labs(title="Choosing the number of clusters",x="k",y=NULL)
ggplot(profiles,aes(PC1,PC2,colour=cluster))+geom_point(alpha=.75,size=2)+
 labs(title=paste("Site profiles: selected k =",best_k),
 subtitle=sprintf("PCA projection explains %.1f%% of scaled-feature variance",
                 100*sum(pca$sdev[1:2]^2)/sum(pca$sdev^2)),
 x="Principal component 1",y="Principal component 2",colour="Cluster")
```

## Distance and algorithm sensitivity

As a sensitivity check, PAM with Manhattan distance is fitted at the same k.
Manhattan sums absolute coordinate differences; Euclidean emphasises larger
coordinate differences. PAM also changes the representative from a mean to an
observed medoid, so any difference cannot be attributed to distance alone.

```{r distance-sensitivity}
pam_fit <- cluster::pam(scaled,k=best_k,metric="manhattan")
# Adjusted Rand index: agreement corrected for chance, invariant to label numbering.
adjusted_rand <- function(a,b) {
  choose2 <- function(x) x*(x-1)/2
  t <- table(a,b)
  observed <- sum(choose2(t))
  r <- sum(choose2(rowSums(t))); c <- sum(choose2(colSums(t)))
  expected <- r*c/choose2(sum(t))
  denom <- (r+c)/2-expected
  if (abs(denom)<1e-12) return(NA_real_)
  (observed-expected)/denom
}
distance_sensitivity <- data.table(
 method=c("K-means / Euclidean","PAM / Manhattan"),
 silhouette=c(cluster_scores[k==best_k,silhouette],pam_fit$silinfo$avg.width))
tab(distance_sensitivity)
ari <- adjusted_rand(profiles$cluster,pam_fit$clustering)
cat(sprintf("Adjusted Rand agreement: %.3f",ari))
tab(as.data.frame.matrix(table(kmeans=profiles$cluster,pam=pam_fit$clustering)))
```

Silhouettes under different metrics are not identical objectives. Assess them
with the profile table and assignment agreement, not just the larger number.
Clusters are descriptive groups, not discovered causal pricing rules.

```{r cluster-findings, results='asis'}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(cluster_centres))) {
  z <- cluster_centres[i]
  cat(sprintf("\n- Cluster %s contains %d sites: average regional-relative price %.2f c/L, price SD %.2f c/L, and average absolute consecutive-day change %.2f c/L.\n",
      z$cluster,z$N,z$relative_mean,z$price_sd,z$mean_abs_change))
}
```

**Choosing k.** WSS falls steadily as k grows, as it always does, so on its own
it does not give a clear elbow. The silhouette is more useful: it rises from
0.38 at k=2 to a peak of 0.46 at k=5, then drops at k=6. At k=2 the split is
basically "Perth versus everyone else" (94% of one cluster is Metro/Peel). From
k=3 a small cluster of 21–25 very expensive remote sites separates out and
survives at every larger k, and from k=4 the Metro sites split into a
strongly cycling group and a cheaper, calmer group. Groups that keep
reappearing as k changes look like real structure rather than noise. I
chose k=5 because it has the best silhouette and every cluster still has at
least 23 sites, so none of them is just a handful of outliers.
