**What the five groups look like** (cluster numbers are only labels; the
region and brand mix comes from `profiles`):

- *Metro price cyclers* (cluster 1, 194 sites, almost all Metro/Peel; mostly BP,
  Ampol and 7-Eleven). These have by far the largest day-to-day moves (about
  6.6 c/L on average) and sit slightly above the regional median. This is the
  weekly cycle from the EDA, seen at site level.
- *Metro discounters* (cluster 4, 283 sites, mostly Metro; Caltex, Reddy Express
  and Vibe are the most common brands). These are cheaper than the median (about
  −2.8 c/L), change price more gently, and raise prices on about a quarter of days.
- *Stable regional sites* (cluster 3, 367 sites, spread across every regional
  area). They are priced close to the local median and rarely change price.
- *Expensive regional sites* (cluster 5, 64 sites, many Independents in the
  Wheatbelt). They are about 18 c/L above the local median, but prices are still
  sticky.
- *Remote, very expensive sites* (cluster 2, 23 sites in Goldfields, Kimberley and
  Pilbara). They average about 118 c/L above the regional median, and prices
  almost never change (mean daily move 0.2 c/L).

So the main "rule" the clustering finds is that two things separate WA stations:
how far they sit from the local median, and whether they take part in the Perth
price cycle. Pricing behaviour is much more about location than brand. The same
brand (BP) shows up in the cycling group, the stable group and the remote group.

On distance measures: I standardised the four features first. Without this,
`relative_mean` (in c/L, with values over 100 for remote sites) would dominate
`increase_rate` (a proportion between 0 and 1), and the clusters would just be
price bands. Euclidean distance with k-means is sensitive to large gaps, which is
partly why the remote group separates so cleanly. With Manhattan distance and PAM
the silhouette is lower (0.37) and the agreement with k-means is moderate
(ARI 0.61). The cross-table shows where they disagree. The two Metro groups are
largely the same under both methods (189 of 194 cyclers and 246 of 283
discounters match). The big stable regional group, however, is split three
ways, and the 23 remote sites no longer form their own cluster: PAM spreads them
across two other groups. This makes sense, because Manhattan distance does not
square the large gap in `relative_mean`, and a medoid is an actual site rather
than a mean that extreme values can pull towards them. So the choice of distance
mostly decides whether extreme sites get their own group. For this question I
prefer the Euclidean version, because the remote stations really do behave
differently.

# Conclusions and limitations

```{r conclusion, results='asis'}
cat(sprintf("The study combined **%s raw records from %d monthly files**, retaining **%s** after quality cleaning (%.4f%% removed).\n\n",
            format(raw_n,big.mark=","),nrow(manifest),format(nrow(d),big.mark=","),100*drop_rate))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(bootstrap))) {
  z <- bootstrap[i]
  cat(sprintf("For %s, recent training minus historical training gives **%.3f test AUC**, with a date-bootstrap interval [%.3f, %.3f].\n\n",
              z$model,z$recent_minus_historical,z$lower,z$upper))
}
cat(sprintf("The site-profile analysis selects **k=%d** by silhouette among the tested values. Use the centroid descriptions to interpret groups, rather than treating cluster numbers as an order.\n",best_k))
```

**Summary of what I found.**

- WA fuel prices are driven by a shared cost level, with stable layers on top
  of it: product (LPG cheapest, diesel/98 RON most expensive), region (Perth
  cheapest, Kimberley about 50 c/L dearer) and, in Perth only, a weekly cycle
  with the cheapest prices on Tuesday.
- The March 2026 shock pushed ULP up by about a third in one month. It barely
  affected the balance of my relative "cheap" label, but it reshuffled which
  stations were cheap for a couple of months and weakened the Perth cycle.
- A station's own track record is the best predictor by far. A smoothed
  "share of cheap days in training" reaches a test AUC of 0.73 (historical) and
  0.84 (recent), well above brand alone (about 0.70). NB and SVM add only
  0.001–0.004 AUC on top, so the simple lookup is nearly as good. Tuning the
  probability cut-off on calibration raises recall (for the recent SVM from 0.70
  to 0.77) at some cost in precision. Oversampling helps less.
- For this question, recent months are clearly better training data than past
  Augusts, mainly because of changes in site coverage and market behaviour after
  the shock, not because of seasonality.
- Stations fall into five behaviour types. Location and participation in the
  price cycle separate them much more than brand does.

The label measures **relative local affordability**, not inflation or historically
cheap fuel. If common price levels change, that alone need not change the label.

Key limits are changing reporting coverage, site-key ambiguity, equal site-day
rather than sales weighting, an SVM trained on only 4,000 rows, repeated
observations of sites, validation/test distribution differences and only one
final test month. Test dates are dependent, so the bootstrap interval is only a
descriptive uncertainty check. More data do not automatically remove these limits.

# Shiny hand-off and reproducibility

The app consumes a compact bundle computed by this notebook. It does not retrain
models when filters change. Exploration filters affect only exploration;
classification uses the fixed ULP population and August 2026 test set. Cluster
views use May–July 2026 site profiles. The app explains these scopes explicitly.

```{r export}
fwrite(evaluation,"outputs/model_metrics.csv")
fwrite(single_scores,"outputs/single_variable_scores.csv")
fwrite(tuning_scores,"outputs/tuning_scores.csv")
fwrite(selected_models,"outputs/selected_models.csv")
fwrite(split_audit,"outputs/split_audit.csv")
fwrite(bootstrap,"outputs/strategy_bootstrap.csv")
fwrite(cluster_scores,"outputs/cluster_k_scores.csv")
fwrite(cluster_centres,"outputs/cluster_profiles.csv")
fwrite(scope_audit,"outputs/model_scope.csv")
cluster_assignments <- lapply(cluster_fits,function(fit) fit$cluster)
bundle <- list(monthly=monthly,daily=daily,brand_month=brand_month,
 plot_sample=plot_sample[,.(date,month_date,product,region,brand,price)],
 coverage=coverage,quality=quality,manifest=manifest,evaluation=evaluation,
 roc=roc_data,single_scores=single_scores,tuning=tuning_scores,
 selected=selected_models,bootstrap=bootstrap,profiles=profiles,
 cluster_scores=cluster_scores,cluster_assignments=cluster_assignments,
 best_k=best_k,cluster_features=cluster_features,scope=scope_audit,
 target_brand=target_brand,
 dates=c(start_date,end_date),created=Sys.time())
saveRDS(bundle,"outputs/dashboard_data.rds")
saveRDS(list(models=fitted_models,predictions=test_predictions,
             parameters=params,selected=selected_models),"outputs/fitted_models.rds")
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()),"outputs/sessionInfo.txt")
stopifnot(nrow(manifest)==44,all(manifest$complete),drop_rate<=.05,!anyNA(missing_audit$missing),
          all(evaluation$AUC>=0 & evaluation$AUC<=1),
          all(evaluation[split=="Test",n]==nrow(test)),
          !anyNA(test_predictions$probability),
          all(test_predictions$date>=test_start),
          nrow(profiles)==length(cluster_assignments[[as.character(best_k)]]))
cat("All end-of-pipeline integrity checks passed.")
```
